semantics.note: Keeps his 'appear/seem' hedge. It is an observation framed as an impression inside a rhetorical question, with no metric, period or named companies.

contract.note: Rightly treats the claim as unscorable. A verdict would need an AI-specific profit measure and a set of companies he never gave.

contract.note: Hedged impression. 'Cut costs' has no metric, and 'never going away' has no deadline. Not adjudicable is fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic S-1 quarterly table, available before the evaluation date. Compute costs rise in dollars but fall as a share of revenue. This cuts both ways and cannot score a hedged claim.

attribution.note: His own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Keeps the condition (a rise of at least 300%), the $80 figure and both strengths: 'most' consumers in general, 'just about every' consumer at $80. The firm 'would' makes it a conditional forecast.

contract.note: The plain reading (Pro $20 as the base price; scored only if a 300%+ rise took effect) is ordinary and fair. Its support and contradiction conditions match 'price out most consumers'.

evidence.note: Third-party tracker, July 2026: Pro still $20. It shows the condition did not happen; it does not contradict the forecast.
Price card verified September 2026: Pro $20, Max $100/$200. The condition was not met. This bears on the antecedent, not the outcome.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast. Both trackers show Claude consumer prices unchanged through September 2026, so the 300% rise never happened. The October prices are unconfirmed but that doesn't matter. A conditional with an unmet antecedent is not scored. The items don't contradict the claim; they are context.
